what: Steve Rosenberg: This year's Victory Day parade in Moscow felt very different

clean_source_blocks.text: The BBC's Russia editor reports from a Red Square with none of the military hardware which the Kremlin normally showcases to project power internationally.

As well as fewer journalists, there were fewer guests in the stands, and fewer world leaders had flown in for the spectacle. But the biggest difference became evident once the parade got under way. There were no tanks, no rocket launchers, no intercontinental ballistic missiles on display - none of the military hardware which the Kremlin normally showcases on Victory Day to project Russian military power on the international stage. That's because this year's parade had been scaled back (hence fewer guests and fewer journalists). The authorities had cited security concerns, fearing Ukraine might target Red Square with drones. President Vladimir Putin will have been reluctant to pare back a parade that is always choreographed to portray Russian strength. But fear of a potential Ukrainian attack forced the change.

I was glad to be there, though. To see for myself what Victory Parade 2026 would look like. As well as fewer journalists, there were fewer guests in the stands, and fewer world leaders had flown in for the spectacle. But the biggest difference became evident once the parade got under way. There were no tanks, no rocket launchers, no intercontinental ballistic missiles on display - none of the military hardware which the Kremlin normally showcases on Victory Day to project Russian military power on the international stage. Russian military servicemen gather during the Victory Day parade That's because this year's parade had been scaled back (hence fewer guests and fewer journalists). The authorities had cited security concerns, fearing Ukraine might target Red Square with drones.

In the end, the parade passed off without incident. There was no attack. A last-minute ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, brokered by Donald Trump, reduced the danger of that. On Friday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky issued a decree "permitting" Russia to hold the parade. Ukraine's trolling wasn't appreciated by Moscow. A Kremlin spokesman commented that Russia didn't need anyone's permission to hold the Victory Parade. And what about all that military hardware I mentioned earlier? We may not have seen it on the square. But we did see it on a screen. Multiple rocket launchers, fighter jets, tanks, submarines and other weaponry flashed up on giant screens that had been set up on Red Square. The Kremlin appears to have decided that if couldn't parade its military hardware in public, a video presentation was the next best thing.

I've attended many Victory Day parades on Red Square.

This year's version felt very different.

In previous years I've had to sprint from the media bus that normally parks up by St Basils' Cathedral, in order to nab a decent spot in the press area at the side of the square.

No running was required this year. There were far fewer journalists at the event. Many international media organisations had not been granted access.

Once I was in position on Red Square, a Russian TV crew came up to me and started filming.

"Steve, you're proof that foreign media have been allowed in," beamed the reporter.

"Not really," I replied. "I can't see any others."

I was glad to be there, though. To see for myself what Victory Parade 2026 would look like.

[Lähde: TIME]
Russian President Vladimir Putin oversaw a pared-down Victory Day parade in Moscow on Saturday, without the usual lines of tanks or missile carriers rolling through Red Square to mark the Soviet Union’s role in defeating Nazi Germany.

Russia’s Defense Ministry blamed the “current operational situation” for the low-key ceremony, a reference to its ongoing invasion of Ukraine. But Russian leaders were also reportedly consumed by the threat posed to the event by Kyiv’s fleet of long-range drones, which have grown increasingly sophisticated in recent years.

The parade has normally served as a show of force from Russia, both to honor the 27 million Soviet citizens who died in World War II, and to demonstrate the nation’s vast military power, including its nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missiles.

payload.title: Moskovan voitonpäivän paraati järjestettiin poikkeuksellisen pelkistettynä
payload.summary: Moskovan vuoden 2026 voitonpäivän paraatissa oli tavallista vähemmän vieraita, toimittajia ja ulkomaisia johtajia. Huomattavin muutos oli raskaan sotakaluston puuttuminen Punaiselta torilta turvallisuushuolien vuoksi.
payload.content:
Moskovassa järjestetty vuoden 2026 voitonpäivän paraati poikkesi selvästi Kremlin aiemmista suurista näytöksistä: Punaisella torilla oli tavallista vähemmän toimittajia, kutsuvieraita ja ulkomaisia johtajia, eikä paraatissa nähty tankkeja, raketinheittimiä tai mannertenvälisiä ohjuksia, joilla Venäjä on usein pyrkinyt esittelemään sotilaallista voimaansa kansainvälisesti.

## Turvallisuushuolet muuttivat paraatin luonnetta

Paraatia oli supistettu, koska Venäjän viranomaiset olivat vedonneet turvallisuushuoliin. Taustalla oli pelko siitä, että Ukraina voisi yrittää iskeä Punaiselle torille drooneilla. Supistaminen näkyi sekä paikalla olleiden toimittajien että katsomossa olleiden vieraiden määrässä.

Voitonpäivän paraati on Venäjälle poliittisesti ja symbolisesti tärkeä tapahtuma, jonka koreografia on perinteisesti rakennettu osoittamaan maan sotilaallista vahvuutta. Presidentti Vladimir Putinille paraatin kaventaminen oli poikkeuksellinen ratkaisu, koska tapahtuma on pitkään ollut osa Kremlin kansainvälistä voimanäyttöä.

Tänä vuonna raskaan kaluston puuttuminen näkyi erityisen selvästi heti paraatin alettua. Punaisella torilla ei marssitettu esiin panssarivaunuja, raketinheittimiä, mannertenvälisiä ballistisia ohjuksia eikä muuta sotakalustoa, jota Kreml on tavallisesti käyttänyt paraatin näyttävimpänä osana.

## Paraati sujui ilman iskua

Lopulta paraati vietiin läpi ilman välikohtauksia. Iskua ei tapahtunut. Vaaraa vähensi viime hetken tulitauko Moskovan ja Kiovan välillä, jonka kerrottiin syntyneen Donald Trumpin välityksellä.

Ukrainan presidentti Volodymyr Zelenskyi lisäsi tilanteeseen poliittista piikittelyä antamalla perjantaina asetuksen, jossa Ukraina ikään kuin salli Venäjän järjestää paraatin. Moskova ei ottanut elettä vastaan huvittuneena: Kremlin edustaja totesi, ettei Venäjä tarvitse keneltäkään lupaa voitonpäivän paraatin pitämiseen.

## Kalusto näkyi näytöillä

Vaikka raskas kalusto puuttui torilta, sitä ei jätetty kokonaan pois esityksestä. Punaiselle torille pystytetyillä suurilla näytöillä esitettiin kuvia ja videoita muun muassa raketinheittimistä, hävittäjistä, tankeista, sukellusveneistä ja muusta aseistuksesta.

Näin Kreml pystyi säilyttämään osan paraatin sotilaallisesta viestistä, vaikka kalustoa ei tuotu fyysisesti paikalle. Ratkaisu korosti samalla sitä, kuinka turvallisuushuolien vuoksi supistettu paraati erosi tavallisesta voitonpäivän voimannäytöstä.

Punaisella torilla ei nähty tankkeja, raketinheittimiä tai mannertenvälisiä ohjuksia.
Paraati sujui ilman iskua, ja sotakalustoa esiteltiin fyysisen paraatin sijaan suurilla näytöillä.

The BBC's Russia editor reports from a Red Square with none of the military hardware which the Kremlin normally showcases to project power internationally.

As well as fewer journalists, there were fewer guests in the stands, and fewer world leaders had flown in for the spectacle. But the biggest difference became evident once the parade got under way. There were no tanks, no rocket launchers, no intercontinental ballistic missiles on display - none of the military hardware which the Kremlin normally showcases on Victory Day to project Russian military power on the international stage. That's because this year's parade had been scaled back (hence fewer guests and fewer journalists). The authorities had cited security concerns, fearing Ukraine might target Red Square with drones. President Vladimir Putin will have been reluctant to pare back a parade that is always choreographed to portray Russian strength. But fear of a potential Ukrainian attack forced the change.

I was glad to be there, though. To see for myself what Victory Parade 2026 would look like. There were no tanks, no rocket launchers, no intercontinental ballistic missiles on display - none of the military hardware which the Kremlin normally showcases on Victory Day to project Russian military power on the international stage. Russian military servicemen gather during the Victory Day parade That's because this year's parade had been scaled back (hence fewer guests and fewer journalists). The authorities had cited security concerns, fearing Ukraine might target Red Square with drones.

In the end, the parade passed off without incident. There was no attack. A last-minute ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, brokered by Donald Trump, reduced the danger of that. On Friday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky issued a decree "permitting" Russia to hold the parade. Ukraine's trolling wasn't appreciated by Moscow. A Kremlin spokesman commented that Russia didn't need anyone's permission to hold the Victory Parade. And what about all that military hardware I mentioned earlier? We may not have seen it on the square. But we did see it on a screen. Multiple rocket launchers, fighter jets, tanks, submarines and other weaponry flashed up on giant screens that had been set up on Red Square. The Kremlin appears to have decided that if couldn't parade its military hardware in public, a video presentation was the next best thing.
